articles.title: Hugh Hefner’s Widow Crystal Harris Asks Jessica Biel to ‘Please Reconsider’ Playing His Wife: ‘I Experienced Sexual, Emotional… Physical Abuse’
articles.summary: Crystal Harris, who was married to Playboy founder Hugh Hefner until his death in 2017, is asking Jessica Biel to reconsider playing a fictional version of H...
articles.body:
Crystal Harris, who was married to Playboy founder Hugh Hefner until his death in 2017, is asking Jessica Biel to reconsider playing a fictional version of Hefner's wife in the upcoming film "Playmates."

After Biel's casting was announced , Harris posted her message to Biel on Instagram , saying "Please reconsider playing Hugh Hefner's wife if this film intends to romanticize him or the Playboy world. I was actually his wife, and I experienced sexual, emotional, financial and physical abuse in that relationship."

Lorraine Nicholson, the daughter of Jack Nicholson, is writing and directing the Searchlight film that also stars Bill Pullman as Hefner as well as Lily-Rose Depp and "The Housemaid's" Indiana Elle.

"Many other woman have come forward with allegations of rape, coercion, drugging and exploitation as well," Harris wrote. "There are also deeply troubling concerns involving minors. I hope everyone involved this film takes the time to listen the women who lived it before helping Hollywood turn it back into nostalgia."

After Hefner's death, Harris revealed her experiences at the "toxic" Playboy mansion in her 2024 memoir "Only Say Good Things: Surviving Playboy and Finding Myself."

According to the synopsis, the "Playmates" movie revolves around "Elle (Elle), a 13-year-old know-it-all who considers the Playboy Mansion her second home, and meets Anna (Depp), one of seven hopefuls vying to be Playmate of the Month. The two form an unlikely friendship and try to help each other get what the other wants most, a magazine cover and a boy." Nicholson has written for magazines about her childhood experiences at the Playboy Mansion.

articles.title: Shakira sorprende a Broncano con su respuesta sobre el dinero: "Entre lo que facturo y lo que gasto, me quedo igual"
articles.standfirst: La intérprete colombiana culminó la semana en ‘La Revuelta’, de La 1 de RTVE
articles.summary: La intérprete colombiana culminó la semana en ‘La Revuelta’, de La 1 de RTVE
articles.body: Este jueves, 8 de octubre, ‘La Revuelta’ cerró una nueva semana con Shakira como invitada. Eso sí, la artista no fue al Teatro Albéniz de Madrid como es habitual, sino que Broncano se desplazó en coche “grabando con un móvil", según indicó, hacia el Estadio Shakira, lugar en el que la colombiana sigue con su puesta de largo en la capital de España. El presentador documentó toda la entrevista hasta llegar al lugar donde la cantante da sus conciertos. Se dirigió hacia ella como la “más grande” y que “la escuchaba desde pequeño”. El programa de este jueves sería editado con un ordenador Lenovo y plano a plano sin ninguna transición, tal y como recalcó. El comunicador del ente público llegó al Estadio Shakira, lo recorrió “haciendo tiempo” en un carro de golf hasta que lo recibió la colombiana. Sin embargo, desde la 17:00 horas que iba a ser la entrevista, Shakira les recibió con retraso, pero la espera mereció la pena, según el comunicador del ente público: “Estar diez minutos con ella es como horas con una persona normal”. De la misma manera, comenzaron hablando del despliegue de la cantante en Madrid y de su último concierto el próximo lunes, 12 de octubre, con el que se despedirá de la ciudad: “Vendrán muchos amigos: Maluma, Beelé, Bizarrap, Dani Martín y más sorpresas que no puedo desvelar”. Asimismo, comentó que su estancia en la ciudad madrileña ha sido “espectacular” y que se “ha sentido muy querida”. Por otro lado, Shakira reveló que en un mes tan solo ha tenido “un día” para descansar que aprovechó para ir a una tienda de minerales con sus amigas de Colombia, añadiendo que se fue “en Uber”. Luego, la artista le dio a Broncano de regalo unas gafas, un chubasquero para invitarle a la Caminata con la Loba, algo que hace la artista en cada concierto antes de empezar. Llegando al tramo final de la entrevista, el presentador reveló que se tenía que ir en avión por un asunto personal y, fue aquí, cuando este le preguntó a Shakira si hacía cosas por amor, a lo que contestó que “muchas”. Además, añadió que le gusta la naturaleza y que diferencia el “pensar” con la “pensadera”: “Pensar es bueno, pero pensar y pensar todo el rato no es nada bueno”. Posteriormente, charlaron de sus hijos y comentó que habla catalán, al igual que el presentador, revelando que hablaba “más catalán en Miami que cuando vivía en Cataluña”. Por último, salió a escena de nuevo su gran despliegue en Madrid, tirándole el presentador una pregunta por el dinero que ganaba, a lo que sentenció Shakira: “Las mujeres facturan, pero también gastan. Entre lo que facturo y lo que gasto, me quedo igual”.

articles.title: Hugh Bonneville plans Suffolk sandwich date with Paddington Bear
articles.summary: Hugh Bonneville says he will visit his movie co-star while promoting a new book in Bury St Edmunds.
articles.body:
Hugh Bonneville has said he will "definitely" spend some time chatting and enjoying a marmalade sandwich with his furry friend Paddington Bear when he visits Suffolk.

The British actor, who has starred in three live-action films with the beloved character, will meet up with his old pal when he promotes his children's book in Bury St Edmunds.

The 62-year-old will be talking at the Bury St Edmunds Literature Festival in the town, which boasts a statue of Paddington on a bench in the arc Shopping Centre.

Bonneville, who was born in Paddington, London, said the county was "very lucky" to have the Peruvian native to lend an ear to tired shoppers when they need a sit down.

"I'm definitely going to have a photo with my friend on the bench," he told the BBC.

"I know he is a much treasured part of so many communities that he has visited and enjoys a sandwich on the bench and then a chat with passers-by.

Aside from his role as Henry Brown in the Paddington film series, Bonneville is perhaps most famous for starring as Robert Crawley, Earl of Grantham in Downton Abbey.

He also appeared alongside Judi Dench, Kate Winslet and Jim Broadbent in the 2001 film, Iris, some of which was filmed in Southwold.

"I remember Kate Winslet and I having a good couple of pints in a pub on the seafront there," Bonneville said.

"So, I'm vaguely familiar with [the area] and I'm looking forward to coming back and dipping my toe, if not into the North Sea, at least into the area."

Bonneville, who has also previously filmed in Dunwich, is returning to Suffolk to promote his latest children's book, Rory Sparkes and the Spy Who Loved Tea.

He will share stories, answer questions and meet fans of his works at the Hunter Club Arts Centre, one of the venues for the Bury St Edmunds Literature Festival.

"I'm really looking forward to it, and it will be lovely to meet families, chat to young readers and writers, and have a natter about Rory Sparkes and reading," he said.

Like the first book in the series, Bonneville's latest offering centres on unlikely young hero Rory who "feels a bit out of place" but learns to embrace his differences.

It is somewhat based on the memories Bonneville has of being a child, which he previously wrote about in a memoir, prompting the idea for a children's book.

He told the BBC he initially scoffed at the idea of writing one but said it has been a "lovely and unexpected departure" from his time on film and TV sets.

"My agent said, 'What about a children's book?' and I said, 'Absolutely not, not my interest, not my area'.

"But then I thought, maybe life in southeast London wasn't as dull as I remembered and so out of that grew Rory Sparkes and the adventures he has with his mates.

"It is largely based on my childhood, so it's been fun to revisit."

articles.title: ‘He called every week’: Ex-Pakistan cricketer reveals how Nana Patekar stood by his mother during illness
articles.summary: The death of veteran actor Nana Patekar has prompted an outpouring of grief beyond India, with members of the Pakistani cricket fraternity also paying
articles.body: The death of veteran actor Nana Patekar has prompted an outpouring of grief beyond India, with members of the Pakistani cricket fraternity also paying tribute to the celebrated performer. Former Pakistan cricketer Basit Ali has shared an emotional account of his long-standing friendship with the actor, remembering how Patekar remained in touch with him and supported his family through difficult periods.Patekar died at the age of 75 on October 8 after suffering a severe cardiac arrest at his residence in Dona Paula, Goa. He was found unconscious and taken to Manipal Hospital, where doctors attempted to revive him with continuous CPR. However, their efforts were unsuccessful, and he was declared dead.As news of his passing spread, Pakistani cricketer Umar Akmal remembered the actor in a social media post, while Basit shared a video reflecting on a personal connection that began in 1994 and continued for decades.Recalling when he first heard about Patekar's death, Basit spoke about the affection he had for the actor and how their association had endured over the years.“Early in the morning I heard sad news. Our very dear brother, friend, and living legend is no longer in this world—Nana Patekar Sahab has passed away. What a person he was; he acted in movies exactly as he was in real life. We had nicknamed Latif as 'Nana'. Because of Nana Patekar, we first talked back in 1994, and it all started from there,” Basit said.The former cricketer then recalled how Patekar would regularly call to check on his family, particularly during the period when his mother was hospitalised. According to Basit, the actor continued to offer emotional support after her death and later enquired about his own health when he suffered a heart problem.“Now there are so many memories. Usually, we spoke once or twice every month. When my mother was alive and in the hospital, Nana Ji called every week. He offered many prayers, talked at length with my mother, and listened to old stories. When my mother passed away, he told me, ‘Hey Basit, take care of yourself now’. And when I had my heart issue and returned home, I received a message asking about my health and telling me to call when I felt better. When I called him back, he inquired about how everything went, including the stent placement,” he added.Basit also remembered the informal conversations they shared about Patekar's films, saying the actor's personality away from the camera was much like the one audiences saw on screen. Their exchanges, he said, were marked by familiarity, warmth and humour.“He was such a wonderful human being. For people who only knew him through movies, he was the exact same person in real life as well. People praised him, and we were fortunate to have many conversations. Sometimes we would ask him about a specific scene in a movie, and he would playfully say, ‘Shut up, what do you know?’. The love and affection he gave as an elder was truly incredible,” he said.The news of Patekar's death was particularly difficult for Basit to accept. He recalled often referring to the actor as a 'young man' because he did not appear to be 75, with Patekar responding jokingly that they were both getting old.“I still can't believe this news. The man did not look 75 years old. I used to always call him ‘young man,’ and he would reply, 'Forget it, both you and I are old now'. It is deeply painful. And I will say one thing here: Nana Ji had as many admirers in Pakistan as he had in India and across the world. People loved him very much," he concluded his video.A career spanning nearly five decadesPatekar was one of the most recognisable names in Hindi and Marathi cinema, building a career that stretched across nearly five decades. He made his Hindi film debut with the 1978 film 'Gaman' before earning widespread recognition for his performances in a range of critically acclaimed and popular films.A defining moment came with Vidhu Vinod Chopra's 'Parinda' in 1989, in which his portrayal of the ruthless crime boss Anna won him the National Film Award for Best Supporting Actor. His filmography also included 'Prahar', 'Angaar', 'Krantiveer', 'Tiranga', 'Khamoshi' and 'Ab Tak Chhappan', among others.His contribution to cinema was recognised with the Padma Shri in 2013, India's fourth-highest civilian award. Away from films, Patekar was also associated with social initiatives, particularly efforts to support farmers and families affected by drought in Maharashtra.The veteran actor remained involved in films in recent years. He was part of 'Housefull 5', which featured Akshay Kumar, Abhishek Bachchan and Riteish Deshmukh, among others. articles.standfirst: En plena promoción de 'Verity' desempolva su pasado con '50 sombras de Grey'
articles.summary: En plena promoción de 'Verity' desempolva su pasado con '50 sombras de Grey'
articles.body: Dakota Johnson está en plena promoción de su nueva película, Verity, y la actriz ha vuelto a dejar una anécdota relacionada con otras interpretaciones que causaron un shock en el ámbito cinematográfico. La actriz que reparte su papel junto a Anne Hathaway y Josh Hartnett, participó en un divertido reto para el canal de YouTube First We Feast. Allí tuvo que elegir entre responder a una pregunta comprometida o enfrentarse a preguntas picantes... La intérprete no se lo pensó dos veces. Aceptó. La cuestión era sencilla: revelar lo más vergonzoso que había hecho para preparar un personaje. Su respuesta desató las risas inmediatas de sus compañeros. En un primer momento, la actriz bromeó asegurando que había sido para Madame Web, aunque enseguida aclaró que en realidad se trataba de la primera entrega de 50 sombras de Grey. "Fue para la primera película. Había una escena de desnudo integral y se suponía que mi personaje nunca se había depilado", desveló Johnson entre risas. La confesión provocó la curiosidad de Anne Hathaway, que le preguntó si no había considerado utilizar una prótesis capilar utilizada habitualmente en cine para este tipo de escenas. La respuesta de Johnson fue tan breve como contundente: "No". Pese a haber participado después en films tan destacados como Suspiria, La hija oscura o Materialistas, Dakota Johnson sigue acumulando titulares vinculados a la saga que la convirtió en una estrella mundial. Y esta última confesión demuestra que el rodaje de 50 sombras de Grey todavía guarda historias capaces de sorprender al público. Johnson también estuvo en el popular programa Saturday Night Live y en él confesó que la película "es un thriller erótico psico-sexual y, ¿sabéis qué? articles.title: US ICE releases Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh from custody
articles.summary: Award-winning filmmaker, detained last month, is released on bond with next hearing set for October 27, campaign says.
articles.body:
The Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency in the United States has released Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh from custody after he was detained on September 24.

The award-winning filmmaker was released on Thursday, two days after he was granted bond, according to a statement by a campaign of his friends and relatives to free him.

However, ICE’s deportation case against Sheikh continues with the next hearing set for October 27, the campaign said.

Sheikh, whose work has explored conflict in his native India-administered Kashmir, was detained by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) as he disembarked from a plane at Dulles International Airport outside Washington, DC, after arriving from California.

The 42-year-old, who lives in Alexandria, Virginia, entered the US on a student visa in 2019 to pursue graduate studies in film at Georgia State University and filed for asylum in 2020.

The campaign said he had a pending asylum application and was authorised to work and live in the US.

The DHS confirmed on Wednesday that Sheikh had been arrested on September 24 and said he “legally entered the US on a temporary basis and illegally overstayed his lawful admittance”.

A pending application does not confer legal status in the US, the DHS said, adding he ⁠will receive due process.

Sheikh’s first feature film, Saffron Kingdom, garnered multiple honours, notably best feature film at the Chicago Filmmakers Awards, Los Angeles Film and Documentary Awards, Melbourne Independent Film Festival, Wake Forest Film Festival and Anatolian International Film Awards.

In 2025, Sheikh was also recognised with the emerging filmmaker activist award at the Teaneck International Film Festival.

His detention came amid a surge in the number of ICE arrests across the US, which hit record levels over the summer. About 50,000 arrests were recorded in July and August.

President Donald Trump’s administration said in August that it was ‌working “to identify ⁠and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the US claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently”.

articles.title: Muere Michael Kearns, actor que rompió el tabú de la homosexualidad en Hollywood y visibilizó el VIH, a los 76 años
articles.standfirst: En los 70, en una sociedad marcada por una fuerte homofobia, hizo pública su condición, convirtiéndose en uno de los rostros más visibles de la comunidad LGBTQ+
articles.summary: En los 70, en una sociedad marcada por una fuerte homofobia, hizo pública su condición, convirtiéndose en uno de los rostros más visibles de la comunidad LGBTQ+
articles.body: Luto en el mundo del cine. Michael Kearns, actor estadounidense conocido por sus apariciones en películas como Doble cuerpo (1984) y en la popular serie Sensación de vivir, ha muerto a los 76 años en Los Ángeles. La noticia ha sido confirmada por personas de su entorno, si bien de momento no han trascendido las causas de su muerte. "Compartimos el pesar por esta pérdida y celebramos el increíble impacto que (Kearns) ha tenido en los movimientos por los derechos LGBTQ y la lucha contra el VIH/sida. Gracias, Michael, por todo lo que le diste a este mundo", se puede leer en un post homenaje en Facebook del Celebration Theatre de Los Ángeles. Con apenas 22 años decidido a abrirse camino en el mundo de la interpretación y llegó a Hollywood. Se convirtió, además, una figura clave por su valentía en momentos en los que hablar públicamente de determinadas cuestiones suponía un enorme riesgo personal y profesional. En los 70, en una sociedad marcada por una fuerte homofobia, hizo pública su homosexualidad, convirtiéndose en uno de los rostros más visibles de la comunidad LGBTQ+ dentro del mundo del espectáculo. Años después volvió a romper barreras al revelar en televisión, en 1991, que era seropositivo, un gesto que contribuyó a dar visibilidad a una enfermedad que entonces seguía rodeada de prejuicios y desinformación. En los años más duros de la epidemia del sida, entre finales de los ochenta y la década de los noventa, Michael Kearns interpretó en distintas producciones a personajes afectados por el VIH. Lo hizo mientras convivía con su propio diagnóstico y sufría la pérdida de amigos y seres queridos a causa de la enfermedad. Más allá de sus papeles en cine y televisión, Kearns deja un legado marcado por su activismo, su compromiso social y su papel como una de las voces que ayudaron a derribar barreras en Hollywood cuando hacerlo no era ni fácil ni habitual.

articles.title: The humble Playdate has become one of gaming’s best deals
articles.summary: As RAMageddon and tariffs have made gaming prohibitively expensive for many, Panic’s Playdate handheld has grown up to become a great deal.
articles.body: The Playdate, Panic’s tiny yellow handheld that launched in 2022, has slowly but surely become a great deal — which is a good thing, because everything else in gaming has only gotten more expensive. Despite being a weird device with a black-and-white screen and a crank jutting out the side, the Playdate has managed to cultivate a strong and constantly growing library of games. And with the handheld’s new season 3 of games, the deal has only gotten better. Playdate’s “seasons” are basically curated collections of games that are released over a short period of time. For season 3, there are eight games in total, with two launching weekly over the span of four weeks. The whole thing costs $39, and the season is off to a pretty good start with two games that are indicative of what the overall Playdate experience is like. [Image: One is called Soggy Froggy, and it’s an arcade game about giving a frog a bath. The little guy sits in a cauldron over a fire, and your job is to keep the water at just the right temperature to keep him warm and cozy. Do nothing and the water quickly heats up, but turn the crank and you can cool things down. If the water gets too hot, well, the poor little froggy boils to death. The goal is to keep him alive for as long as possible, making it a game about chasing a high score that’s both cute and morbid. I can’t stop playing. The other new release is a dungeon-crawling RPG called Gloom Gate. Here the goal is to traverse a sprawling castle, defeating all kinds of monsters and gathering gear and experience points to get stronger. What’s most notable about the game, though, is its 3D graphics, which feel like they shouldn’t be possible on the underpowered Playdate. In each battle you enter into a small arena with an enemy, and you have to dodge, parry, and attack while keeping a close eye on your stamina, which depletes with every action you take. It’s kind of like a stripped-down version of Dark Souls (there are even campfires to rest at), but it also really reminds me of Epic’s long-lost mobile series Infinity Blade, which was similarly a technical showcase centered around surprisingly deep combat. [Image: The full lineup for season 3 hasn’t been revealed yet, but it’ll also include a word game, hide-and-seek for two players on the same handheld, and a classic Mac-style point-and-click adventure (a trend I can really get behind). It seems like there’s going to be quite a bit of variety, and that really captures what the first few years of the Playdate have been like so far. Between its seasons and the Catalog store, as well as the ability to sideload games from platforms like Itch.io, the handheld has built up a very strong lineup that covers just about every genre you can think of: daily puzzle games, demonic pinball, Monument Valley-style adventures, even an MMO. It’s impressive both how much developers have been able to squeeze out of the device as well as how expertly Panic has managed to curate the platform. Every time I check out the shop it seems like there’s something new and interesting to try. The Playdate hasn’t been totally immune to the steadily more expensive nature of the world. Last year, it got $30 more expensive due to increased production costs. But when compared to everything else going on, the current $229 price tag feels like a drop in the bucket, particularly when most new games for the Playdate only cost a few bucks. For comparison, the special edition of Grand Theft Auto VI — which, to be clear, doesn’t even include the game — costs $399.99. Obviously the Playdate isn’t a one-to-one replacement for a new PlayStation or Switch. You can’t play the latest big-name releases — you’re going to miss out on a very busy November, for instance — and outside of a few titles, it’s a mostly solitary experience. But even still, in an era of rising costs and formulaic games, the Playdate remains a breath of fresh air, a comparatively affordable platform that’s home to games that are inventive and surprising. And it’s a platform that only seems to be getting better with time.

articles.title: Michael Douglas reacts to wife Catherine Zeta-Jones saying she has ‘no intention’ of reading his memoir
articles.summary: The “Wall Street” actor had a brilliant response.
articles.body:
Michael Douglas reacted after wife Catherine Zeta-Jones said she had "no intention" of reading his memoir.

The actor explained that he lived a whole other life before they got married, which is detailed in One Helluva Ride .

Douglas' memoir was published earlier this week.

Michael Douglas really does not want wife Catherine Zeta-Jones reading his recently published memoir.

During Douglas' Thursday interview on Jimmy Kimmel Live , host Jimmy Kimmel brought up Zeta-Jones' Today interview earlier that day, during which the actress said she has "no intention of reading" about her husband.

"I wondered if you felt that was for the best," Kimmel asked on Thursday. Douglas replied, "Oh, yeah," which received some laughs from the crowd.

"Look, I mean, we got a 25-year age difference," the Wall Street actor continued. "I opened up and mentioned the book and exposed the fact that Kathleen Turner and I had an affair when we were making Romancing the Stone . Catherine was 7 years old at the time and wouldn't know her husband for 25 years ahead."

Douglas added, "I think she's had to accept the fact that having this kind of age difference, you may have had a life before you ever seen her for the first time."

Kimmel joked that Zeta-Jones thought Douglas "was a virgin" before they got married. "Correct," Douglas replied. "She told you that?"

Get your daily dose of entertainment news, celebrity updates, and what to watch with our EW Dispatch newsletter .

Douglas and Zeta-Jones have been married since 2000 and share two children.

One Helluva Ride , which was published on Tuesday, includes several of Douglas' romantic trysts through the years. Many of them took place during his first marriage to Diandra Luker, to whom he was married from 1977 to 2000. Douglas has confirmed that he got several women's permission to discuss their romantic pasts before writing the memoir.

Kimmel wondered on Thursday if anyone told Douglas that he couldn't write about their relationship. "I'll never say," the Oscar winner replied.

Douglas and Turner's past affair has continued to make headlines, especially since they kept it a secret for 40 years. While appearing on SiriusXM's Andy Cohen Live earlier this week, Douglas revealed exactly what he said when asking for permission to publish details about their romance during production on the 1984 hit. (Turner was married to Jay Weiss from 1984 to 2007.)

"I asked her, I said, 'Look, I think it's, you know, time,'" the Fatal Attraction star explained. "Kathleen had gone through a marriage then herself and all of that, so I thought it was time to put it in because there's so many good stories and have that one included."

He added, "She said, 'Yeah.' She said, 'Fine.' So, I told that story, and then I got permission and said, 'Kathleen, do I tell the rest of some of the stories that we've had in One Helluva Ride ?' And she said, 'Okay.'"

While Douglas continues to field questions about his relationship with Turner, she is unbothered by the affair reveal.

"Good heavens what a fuss about something 40 years ago!" the actress told Entertainment Weekly 's sister site PEOPLE in a statement . "I love Michael and I look forward to enjoying the book."

One Helluva Ride is out now. Watch Douglas' full Jimmy Kimmel Live interview above.

articles.title: New movies to watch this weekend: See 'The Social Reckoning' in theaters, rent or buy 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day,' stream 'Animals' on Netflix
articles.summary: Our critic's take on the week's biggest movie releases — including Aaron Sorkin's follow-up to "The Social Network."
articles.body:
Welcome to Trust Me, I Watch Everything , a weekly guide to notable new movies opening or becoming available each Friday.

This week brings two buzzy theatrical releases: The Social Reckoning , a follow-up to The Social Network that has Jeremy Strong taking over the Mark Zuckerberg role from Jesse Eisenberg, and Other Mommy , Jessica Chastain's jump-scare-heavy horror. (If you're looking for more chills this Halloween season, consult my spine-tingling recommendations here .)

If you'd prefer a movie night at night, you can now rent or buy Spider-Man: Brand New Day — though, given it's the highest-grossing film in U.S. box office history, it stands to reason most folks have already seen it. And over on streaming, Ben Affleck is doing double duty as star and director of the kidnapping drama Animals , while John Cena and Jessica Biel try to milk an action movie out of Matchbox cars.

Why I was underwhelmed: The Social Network is one of the great films of the 2010s. Written by esteemed playwright and screenwriter Aaron Sorkin, directed by auteur David Fincher and featuring an instantly iconic score from Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, the movie depicts the dawn of a new hyper-digital era. Years later, it maintains an eerie prescience.

Given all that, it's not entirely fair to compare The Social Network to its new sequel, The Social Reckoning . But the movie's complete lack of visual style and embarrassingly generic score are, unfortunately, constant reminders that David Fincher and the Nine Inch Nails boys are nowhere to be found this time. Instead, the new movie is written and directed by Aaron Sorkin — and is a case study in the impact a talented director has on a film, even when the writer brings a lot to the table. (Oddly enough, Fincher was busy making a sequel to another beloved movie, Quentin Tarantino's Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, despite having no involvement with the original.)

The Social Reckoning follows Frances Haugen , a young Facebook engineer played by 2025 Best Actress Osca r winner Mikey Madison, who crosses paths with Jeff Horwitz, a Wall Street Journal reporter played by The Bear heartthrob Jeremy Allen White, and winds up blowing the whistle on the social network's most guarded secrets. Essentially, it's a journalism movie about the Facebook Files , a series of investigative reports from the Journal that revealed internal findings about the company's platforms, including indictations that Instagram had negative effects on teen mental health and how its algorithm exposed users to misinformation and extremist content.

There has been ample material to work with in the years since we last checked in with Mark Zuckerberg, who is now played by notoriously intense method actor Jeremy Strong, in an impressively strange performance that makes Zuck out to be more space alien than human and someone who prizes profits and growth over everything. The Facebook Files revelations made The Social Network an even more important movie in retrospect, and you can feel Reckoning straining for the same status. The problem is, you can't set out to write an Important Movie, and Sorkin doesn't seem willing to leave that judgment to the masses.

There's a ham-fisted quality to the way Sorkin connects characters in his movie to actual events — I didn't expect the movie to heavily involve Jan. 6, though I can see why it does — and despite its earnestness, there were chuckles at my screening when a minor character introduced early in the film reappeared to drive home a key message. Though I appreciate a movie tackling important issues like what Facebook has historically gotten away with, the treatment here is simply too pat and on-the-nose.

The biggest problem with The Social Reckoning lies outside the film: Our current reality undercuts the entire notion that there was any sort of "reckoning" for Facebook or Zuckerberg. Sure, people found out about their misdeeds, but it only had a minimal effect on Meta's bottom line , and the company is still thriving today.

The movie desperately wants a happy ending, one in which you can imagine a character punching the air in a cinematic moment of victory, a gesture that rings hollow if you are alive in the world today. The Social Reckoning looks and feels more like a cheap knockoff TV movie follow-up to The Social Network than a real, expensive movie made by the same studio that produced the original. It tells an important story, but without any of the verve that made Fincher's film stand the test of time.

What other critics are saying: Reviews are mixed. Robbie Collin at the Telegraph writes that Sorkin "has made a doggedly conventional and old-fashioned journalistic procedural." Time's Stephanie Zacharek was kinder, writing, "Frances Haugen is the conscience and the true hero of The Social Reckoning , and Sorkin knows it. He practically hands the movie over to Madison, and even in a movie filled with talking, it's her stalwart yet unassuming presence that makes it sing."

How to watch: The Social Reckoning is now playing in theaters nationwide .

Why it's a mixed bag: The creepy trailer for Other Mommy debuted ahead of Universal's big summer blockbuster The Odyssey, which means that damn near everybody became suddenly very aware of the Jessica Chastain-starring horror movie. It ended up catching unsuspecting moviegoers off guard with a pretty shocking jump scare.

A young girl forms a relationship with a sinister entity in her home that looks uncannily like her own mother — I'm seeing double! Four Jessica Chastains! — drawing her into a terrifying and increasingly dark world. The Other Mommy entity wants the girl to let her into the girl's heart, presumably to take over her body and assume human form.

If that sounds like it's ripe material for a "metaphorror" movie, a horror movie whose terrors are actually standing in for some sort of real-world trauma, you'd be correct. This attempt at realism clashes with the dark fairy tale dream — or rather, nightmare — logic that rears its head throughout.

Rob Savage directs the hell out of it, his whacked-out visual language and swirling camerawork rendering a shot of a girl rifling through a freezer interesting, and deploying a 360-degree tracking shot to put us in the POV of a girl on a tire swing. Transitions between scenes are similarly gonzo.

I actually found all the spooky stuff associated with the entity, like the way it wears people like skin suits and the uniquely chilling disintegration that occurs when it changes form, pretty effective.

The biggest problem with Other Mommy is that it's all over the place. It takes an Insidious detour for a bit, turns onto the It freeway , and its ever-expanding nightmare logic gives way to some A Nightmare on Elm Street- style side quests, which are effective but don't exactly jibe with the reality of the scenes. The rules here are just inconsistent — the entity can apparently do anything to anyone, even at a crowded party — in a way that's distracting more than it is disturbing.

I appreciated Other Mommy taking some bold swings and trying to get at very real issues regarding motherhood, but it overcomplicates things with human melodrama that feels unnecessary and underdeveloped. An expositional monologue that flatly explains the correlations between the entity and the little girl's worldview just bogs everything down.

Other Mommy works better as a series of horror set pieces than it does as a coherent treatise on the loss of identity and freedom that occurs when one chooses to become a mother. And that's fine, though I fear the movie gives away its biggest jump scare in the marketing, and it never really matches that pure shock energy again.

What other critics are saying: Reviews are not kind. Variety's Siddhant Adlakha says it's "among the most limp and ineffectual works to grace the screen this year, misfiring in every direction, including and especially its tone." Richard Lawson at the Hollywood Reporter writes, "The film is missing a sense of dreadful build-up that might help its scares sink in deeper. As is, Savage's film is an attractive but mostly vacuous collection of jumpy bits and half-baked mythology."

How to watch: Other Mommy is now playing in theaters nationwide.

The biggest release: Spider-Man: Brand New Day

Why I didn't like it: It takes about three minutes before Spider-Man is shown next to a Little Caesars box, and a couple more minutes for him to order another one. A few minutes later, he's framed next to some Bero, Tom Holland's booze-free beer, at the bodega. We get it — this is corporate-branded big business more than it is entertainment, merely a vehicle to sell more whatever. Call it Spider-Man: New Brand Day!

This is certainly an annoying thing to complain about — I remember all of Tobey Maguire's Sony-branded gear from the Sam Raimi movies, but having a Sony laptop doesn't break immersion; flashing a bright orange pizza box twice in what feels like 90 seconds does. It also really speaks to the major problem with the modern-day MCU: This movie feels as impersonal as possible, and the entire endeavor is so clearly a means to an end.

It's emblematic of another issue that plagues Marvel: Even when it's not doing blatant in-your-face product placement, it's doing tacit product placement. What is the inclusion of Frank Castle if not an in-movie ad for The Punisher, now streaming on Disney+? As someone who checked out of the MCU right around the time they pivoted to "You better watch this Disney+ show if you want the full experience," I have no idea why Jon Bernthal's very silly take on The Punisher is in this movie, other than some brand synergy play. I love the guy, but his performance reeks of "this belongs on television."

The villain, kept secret in the marketing, feels similarly shoehorned in, but clearly ties this movie to the next big Marvel release, Avengers: Payday, or whatever it's called. The entire modus operandi of the MCU is to keep viewers invested in the next thing; otherwise, the whole project crumbles.

This helps explain why Tom Holland's MCU Spider-Man, despite a decade as the character and four mainline movies , has never really felt like the star of his own show, even though Spidey is the most popular superhero in the world. In Homecoming, he's introduced as Tony Stark Jr.; in No Way Home, he literally gets sidelined so past Spider-Men (Spiders-Man?) can get some applause.

In the self-serious slog that is Brand New Day, which announces itself as such with a more melancholic Marvel Studios logo than usual, decent storytelling and stakes are nowhere to be found; things just happen arbitrarily as the movie lumbers along with zero tension. Don't confuse "it has no story" for "it has no plot" — the movie is all plot! (Here, most of it centers on everyone — even his loved ones — forgetting all about Peter Parker as he confronts a new villain.)

When the movie is actually engaging with the characters we care about, like MJ and Ned, it's far better for it. More often than not, it's off on some tangent with Frank Castle. Or teasing out the villain, who is so obvious from the jump that all the laborious build-up lacks tension, no matter how cool some of the mind-control stuff gets. By the end, it's clear Spider-Man has taken a backseat in a Spider-Man movie yet again. Call me old-fashioned, but I think Spider-Man movies should be about Spider-Man and not a backdoor pilot for something else.

What other critics are saying: It's very well-reviewed overall. Stephanie Zacharek at Time says the film, "at the very least, shows some awareness that actors, and not excessive, soul-killing special effects, are what will keep drawing us to the movies." Rolling Stone's David Fear was more on my wavelength, however, writing that "the movie keeps getting tangled in a complicated web of its own making, one that feels all too familiar after several decades of superhero cinema sucking up the cultural oxygen."

How to watch: Spider-Man: Brand New Day is available to rent or buy on Apple TV , Prime Video and other VOD platforms.

Why I liked it, with reservations: Onslaught sees filmmaker Adam Wingard returning to his roots, giving up a Godzilla vs. Kong- sized studio blockbuster budget to instead make a relatively cheap and dirty '80s-style exploitation movie throwback, complete with John Carpenter movie font for its opening titles. Wingard has teased that the movie takes place in the same town as his cult favorite The Guest, and both feature Dan Stevens in different key roles. But make no mistake: Onslaught is 100% Adria Arjona's movie.

Onslaught is a delightfully unsubtle exploitation action horror movie about a U.S. government that's controlled by Nazis, killing its own citizens and manipulating its veterans. When a rogue squad of genetically engineered super-soldiers breaks loose in the desert, a badass Army sniper (Arjona) must unleash hell to protect her young daughter. The three super-soldiers are given the slasher-movie villain treatment; they're unstoppable killing machines who act like "heat-seeking missiles" toward whatever their objective may be. Imagine The Terminator, but there are three of them!

It's a lot of fun if you're into this sort of thing, and the constantly pulsing imitation John Carpenter synth score makes it feel bigger than it actually is. The biggest issue with the movie is entirely self-imposed: It prominently features a countdown clock ticking down to a sequence that ultimately doesn't live up to expectations when time runs out.

It feels like it's missing a barnburner finale, even if the gunplay and action are otherwise satisfying enough. Had the movie not insisted upon repeatedly saying "buckle up, audience, you're not going to believe this s**t," maybe the ending would've been thrilling enough. But after all that build-up, it can't help but feel like a bit of a letdown.

There's so much going on in the periphery of this movie. Rebecca Hall's character is a hoot but underutilized, Drew Starkey's goofy subplot really made me laugh but felt misplaced and Dan Stevens's evil Nazi doctor looks like an anime villain. It's a shame that it all comes off a little too straightforward, despite these occasional wacky elements.

Onslaught is perfectly entertaining for what it is, though it feels like the movie fails on its own terms by not living up to the expectations it set up for itself. It's as if Babe Ruth stepped up to the plate, called his shot and then hit a double. You'd appreciate that he got on base, but you'd probably be a little underwhelmed.

What other critics are saying : The reviews skew positive, but there are plenty of naysayers. T he Daily Beast's Nick Schager calls it "a hodgepodge of everything genre fans adore." Jake Coyle at the AP, however, writes that, "Even though Onslaught begins with a clock that's already ticking below 12 hours, the movie takes its time leading to a bloody finale that isn't quite worth the drumbeat."

How to watch: Onslaught is available to rent or buy on Apple TV , Prime Video and other VOD platforms.

Insidious: Out of the Further : The sixth entry in this long-running franchise features some of the most memorable scare sequences in the entire series. Gemma, a young mother raising her daughter in the house where she grew up, discovers she can travel to The Further, the purgatorial realm of lost souls at the heart of the Insidious universe. When something evil comes after her, Gemma discovers an ability that changes everything: She doesn't just enter The Further; she can bring back what lives there to the real world. Once the demons realize her power, our world becomes their playground. It's a clever standalone entry that stays true to the spirit of these movies and, more importantly, delivers spooky set pieces one after another. Read my full review here . Rent or buy.

Fall 2: Deadpoint : 2022's Fall made your palms sweaty in the way all good survival horror does. The situation in which two girls are stuck 2,000 feet in the air on a radio tower is inherently terrifying, and the movie succeeds despite its cheapness and occasional bad CGI and phony green-screen effects. It largely looks convincing and made me yell out loud multiple times. If you're even mildly afraid of heights, it'll mess you up. Fall 2: Deadpoint works for the same reasons, and really pushes the limits of how silly a B-movie can get as long as it's delivering the goods. But it's brisk and has enough thrills to recommend to fans of the original and/or the genre . Read my full review here . Rent or buy.

Colony: The director of the South Korean hit Train to Busan is back with a new zombie movie that does just enough with the genre to make it feel exciting again. Trapped inside a sealed building during a deadly bioterrorist attack, a desperate group of survivors must navigate growing panic and betrayal as they fight to stay alive. The novel idea here is that the zombies are a hivemind, so when one zombie learns new information about how to attack its prey, all the zombies "update" with that intel in real time. That twist, plus the idea of an evil villain controlling the zombies and starting the outbreak itself, gives it a freshness other zombie films lack. Colony also pays homage to genre classics, from George Romero to Resident Evil and The Last of Us, while charting its own path. It's a blast! Rent or buy.

Why you should just watch High and Low instead : Ben Affleck's Animals, despite not being credited as such, is absolutely a remake of Akira Kurosawa's classic High and Low, which, oddly, was already remade just last year by Spike Lee with Denzel Washington starring. Steven Soderbergh also did a miniseries a few years ago called Full Circle, loosely inspired by the 1963 Japanese favorite.

Given all that, Animals never makes a case for its existence in a world where this exact story has been told many times. When the son of an L.A. mayoral candidate is kidnapped, he and his wife have a few hours to come up with the ransom payment. With most of their money spent on his political campaign, they have to get their hands dirty and expose a side of their lives they never intended to see the light of day.

The plot unfolds exactly as you'd expect it to if you've seen the original, the Spike Lee one or the Soderbergh series — so spoiler alert, I suppose, if you've managed to avoid all of those. It turns out they kidnapped the wrong kid, and now the family's very emotional ordeal becomes more of a moral dilemma, as Affleck's character must decide whether he wants to give away all his money to save someone else's child.

The elements unique to Affleck's West Coast edition of High and Low are the specifics surrounding the kidnapped child's family. It's the son of Affleck's housekeeper and her undocumented immigrant husband who gets snatched, which poses a political liability for his mayoral candidate character.

These details are meant to complicate things and show how fake and hypocritical politicians can be, I suppose, but the movie doesn't engage with that meaningfully for very long. It's all just so flat.

Animals may entertain if you've never seen the original High and Low or any of its imitators. For the rest of us, it's an unsatisfying return to the material that brings nothing newly compelling to the table.

What other critics are saying : Reviews aren't super kind. AP's Jake Coyle writes, "Affleck is a savvy and thoughtful filmmaker who can deftly weave human stories, genre mechanics and social issues together. But Animals feels narratively underpowered and melodramatically forced." Jesse Hassenger at the Guardian writes, "This is a movie that just wants to get the job done with frictionless likability, with seemingly no one inquiring about why."

How to watch: Animals is now streaming on Netflix.

Why it's a mixed bag: Matchbox: The Movie is perhaps a foreboding sign of what's to come under David Ellison's Skydance, which produced this movie before it became the conjoined home of Paramount and Warner Bros.

It's a cynical, crass and often embarrassing attempt to turn a child's toy into a viable franchise IP à la Barbie, another Mattel production. In this case, the children's playthings are Matchbox toy cars, and the way the movie incorporates them is almost impressively lazy, especially considering how quickly all those details are dropped entirely.

After hostiles abduct former soldier Sean Walker (John Cena) to locate a nuclear warhead, the CIA suspects his involvement. Later, Walker and his childhood friends (Jessica Biel, Sam Richardson, Arturo Castro and Teyonah Parris) plot to reclaim the bomb and clear their names.

If you're wondering, "What the hell does this have to do with Matchbox?" the answer is "Not much!" The film opens with the characters as children, and the kid version of Cena's character aims to win the heart of Child Jessica Biel by … buying her the exact Matchbox car that she desperately wants.

Thankfully, her uncle, played by the wonderful Bill Camp, is there to provide ad copy, telling us the company's origins with dialogue about how the very first Matchbox car was actually a gift. Something about "a father wanting to make his daughter smile," but because of the rules of her school, he had to make the car small enough to fit in a matchbox, so he got creative.

Cut to adulthood, and when this uncle dies, these childhood friends come together and somberly place Matchbox cars on his grave. Cena, who is now some sort of mercenary, shows up and drags everyone into action set pieces.

The reason this review isn't a total evisceration and is instead more of a light pan is that they got action director Sam Hargrave, the guy behind Netflix's Extraction movies with Chris Hemsworth, to make it. The action here is actually pretty good and occasionally exciting, delivering far better thrills than your average streaming-era A-list mockbuster. It's much slicker than you'd think it would be, and the comedy between the friends works fairly well too, especially as the set pieces get bigger and crazier and the non-action heroes get to do action hero stuff.

Unfortunately, none of that masks the fact that this is just a generic globe-trotting action-adventure movie with some marketing copy sprinkled in. Anytime it strains for emotional resonance, it falls flat. It's a sad state of affairs that the easiest way to get an expensive action movie made these days is to make it sponsored content and toss it on streaming.

Matchbox: The Movie delivers where it counts, and if you're in the mood for some expensive-looking action, you can do far worse while scrolling through Apple TV's original movies catalog. It remains funny that Matchbox factors into this so little that it plays like they only retroactively called it that after the company got wind of their upcoming Generic Action Movie.

What other critics are saying: They're largely meaner than I was, but some agree it's better than you'd think. Ben Lee at the Guardian writes, "A plasticky, unenthused Cena is stuck in autopilot once again while a similarly flat Biel, bizarrely choosing this as her first film in almost a decade, makes zero effort to convincingly play anyone but herself." TheWrap's William Bibbiani writes, " Matchbox: The Movie is one of the most entertaining generic streaming action comedies, which says very little."

How to watch: Matchbox: The Movie is now streaming on Apple TV.

Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger: I never got into Oasis and only know the hits, but that doesn't matter in the slightest here somehow. I found this to be a deeply moving and emotional experience about the transcendent joy of seeing your favorite band live and the importance of the communal concertgoing experience. Fans are in for a real treat! Now streaming on Disney+ .

V/H/S/Mixtape: The latest entry in the long-running found-footage horror anthology series is unfortunately a weaker one, especially coming off the heels of the excellent V/H/S/Halloween. The first short is notable for featuring some Jim Henson puppets, but the premise is tired and familiar. The rest are completely forgettable, except for the last short, Death Tone, directed by RZA, which features gore so nasty that I had to look away. Your mileage may vary! Now streaming on Shudder .

Disclosure Day: Disclosure Day was positioned not just as a major summer blockbuster, but as the return of the Steven Spielberg summer blockbuster, 51 years after Jaws. Audiences were unfortunately primed for disappointment, as Spielberg's latest extraterrestrial adventure is far from his greatest. Read my full review here . Now streaming on Peacock .

That's all for this week! We'll see you next Friday, when the big releases are Street Fighter, Whalefall and Sense and Sensibility .

articles.title: Filmmaker Mehul Kumar, who did three films with Nana Patekar, on his close association with the volatile actor: 'He used to lead such a healthy life, had only one problem, temper'
articles.summary: Filmmaker Mehul Kumar, who directed Nana Patekar in ‘Tiranga’, ‘Krantiveer’ and ‘Kohram’, says he still finds it hard to believe the actor is gone.
articles.body: Filmmaker Mehul Kumar, who directed Nana Patekar in ‘Tiranga’, ‘Krantiveer’ and ‘Kohram’, says he still finds it hard to believe the actor is gone. Remembering their close family bond, he recalls how Nana agreed to ‘Tiranga’ when stars like Rajinikanth refused, how he handled the film’s moody leads, and how Nana had even agreed to do ‘Krantiveer 2’.Nana Patekar is gone?It is very hard to believe I used to talk to him. And he used to lead such a healthy life. In eating and drinking. He had only one problem. Temper. But he was very kind heart. We had such a good family relationship. I am the only director he did three films with. He used to say, I have only one director with whom I never had any problem. And that is Mehul Kumar. We did 'Tiranga', 'Krantiveer', and 'Kohram'.'Tiranga' and 'Krantiveer' were blockbusters. But 'Kohram' didn’t work?Yes, but in Kohram, Nana Ji and Amit Ji were together for the first time. What a pair they were.So tell me, how did your association with them start?When 'Tiranga's casting was going on, at that time, no one was ready to do the role. I asked Rajinikanth; he refused. Naseeruddin Shah Saab also refused. Then our publicity designer, Studio Link, suggested Nanaji. I went to his Lokhandwala house and told him the story. And he agreed. He liked the story very much. He had only one reservation.What was that?Nanaji said he had never worked with Raj Kumar, known for his moodiness. ‘I am doing the film, but if Mr Raj Kumar interferes on the set, I will leave the set and not come back.’I have to praise you for your courage. Both Nana and Raj Kumar were famous for their moodiness?I had absolutely no problem with them. 'Tiranga' was completed in six months and became a super hit. In the beginning, they didn't sit together. But they shot that song, 'Pee Le Together'; they came very close. Nana was the backbone of 'Tiranga' and then 'Krantiveer'.How did Nana get along with Mr Bachchan?When I started making 'Kohram', which was a film on terrorism, I told Amit Ji the story. Amit Ji said okay. Then I told Nana. Nana also said okay. Amit Ji asked me, ‘I am doing this film for you. There won't be any problem with Nana. Because his reputation is everywhere.' I told Amitji, ‘This is the third film with Nana and my second with you (we had worked together earlier in. You don’t worry.’ There was no problem.How did you make two temperamental actors like Raj Kumar and Nana work together so peacefully?I told them the story. I told them, 'If you have any problem, we can discuss it.' We won't make any changes.Were you in touch with him?Yes. Family relations with Nana. My wife used to tie a rakhi to him. Every Raksha Bandhan. Whenever he wanted to eat, he used to call home and say, 'I am coming today.' When his film was released, we met in the premiere. Anil Sharma's film. He asked me to click a photo of all three of us. My wife is on one side, and I am on the other.You were going to work with Nana again?I had finalised the subject for 'Krantiveer 2'. articles.summary: The Gauhati High Court on Friday granted bail to Amritprava Mahanta, a co-singer of the late Zubeen Garg, in the case related to his death.
articles.body: The Gauhati High Court on Friday granted bail to Amritprava Mahanta, a co-singer of the late Zubeen Garg, in the case related to his death. She is the first accused in the matter to get bail from the court.Bail granted on a bond of Rs 50,000According to an ANI report, Special Public Prosecutor Ziaul Kamar said the court allowed bail on a bond of Rs 50,000. The order came after Mahanta moved a bail petition before the High Court. She had been arrested by the Special Investigation Team (SIT) of Assam Police in 2025, after being questioned for several hours.How Zubeen Garg passed awayThe singer died in Singapore on September 19, 2025, in a scuba diving accident. This was a day before he was due to perform at the Northeast India Festival. Shyamkanu Mahanta, who has organised the festival since 2013, was also arrested after Garg’s death.Supreme Court’s direction on the trialIn August, the Supreme Court asked the Assam government to ensure a careful and speedy trial against Shyamkanu Mahanta, who faces criminal charges in the case. A bench of Justices BV Nagarathna and R Mahadevan was told that the trial was being held daily and that several key witnesses were expected to depose in the coming weeks. Justice Nagarathna said orally that the court was keeping the State under pressure to move the trial forward and that the bench would review the progress when the matter was heard again.Arguments in courtSenior advocate Siddharth Dave, appearing for Shyamkanu Mahanta, argued that Garg was an adult who willingly boarded a boat, went into the sea wearing a life jacket and then drowned. He added that his client was not present when the incident took place.Dave also questioned the claim that Mahanta conspired to cause Garg’s death by not looking after him properly or by giving him alcohol. He said Garg was an adult and Mahanta could not be blamed for his choice to drink.The State, however, maintained that Garg’s death was not an accident and that the prosecution had material pointing to a conspiracy.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Watch: Mountain biker takes 12.46-foot vertical drop onto a small target
articles.summary: An Austrian mountain biker dropped 12.46 feet from an elevated platform to crush a small cardboard box with his back tire and set a world record.
articles.body:
Oct. 9 (UPI) -- An Austrian mountain biker dropped 12.46 feet from an elevated platform to crush a small cardboard box with his back tire and set a world record in the process.

Mario Neurauter attempted the stunt at Bike Republic Sölden Festival in September 2025, and managed to set the Guinness World Record for the highest vertical drop on a bicycle on to a target (male).

Neurauter rode his bike off an elevated platform 12.46 over the ground and managed to land his back tire on a small red box, which he successfully crushed.

"I wasn't scared, but I knew that hitting the box would be tricky. I hadn't trained for it specifically, so I didn't know how many attempts it would take. In the end, it worked out pretty well," he told Guinness World Records.

Neurauter also attempted the Guinness World Records for the highest vertical drop on a bicycle and highest 360 vertical drop on a bicycle onto a target during the same weekend, but evidence from those attempts is still being reviewed by the record-keeping organization.
